La réchauffement climatique se fait sent: Global warming is being felt in Tête-à-la-Baleine, on the Côte-Nord.
Cette année, la crise climatique s’est f: This year, the climate crisis hit Canada hard.
Les températures en Colombie-Britannique: Temperatures in British Columbia neared 50 degrees Celsius, breaking records. Because of this extreme heat, thousands of forest fires raged across Western Canada, destroying natural habitats in their path and displacing communities. Faced with such a critical situation, do our elected officials have ambitious plans to tackle the climate emergency?

Le Parti conservateur propose un compte: The Conservative Party is proposing a personal carbon savings account. Every time a consumer buys hydrocarbon-based fuel, $20 per tonne of fuel will be paid into their personal savings account, an amount they can use to live a greener life. The Green Party is proposing a carbon tax that would rise by $25 per tonne from 2022 to 2030. The Conservative, Liberal, New Democratic, Bloc Québécois and Green parties are all committed to reaching carbon neutrality, that is, reaching a zero-emission pollution target.

As for the Liberal and New Democratic parties, they promise to reach carbon neutrality by 2050.

Les partis conservateurs, libéraux, et v: The Conservative, Liberal and Green parties intend to support and work with Indigenous land guardians to create Indigenous Protected and Conserved Areas (IPCAs).
Les partis conservateurs, libéraux, néo-: The Conservative, Liberal, New Democratic, Bloc Québécois and Green parties are committed to making the transition to green energy. Le Parti néo-démocrate promet des prêts: The New Democratic Party promises low-interest loans to Canadians and support measures for tenants and low-income households to improve the energy efficiency of their housing. It is also committed to making sure every new building constructed is carbon neutral by 2025. The Green Party is committed to creating a national green retrofit program for residential buildings, supporting organizations that offer green renovations, and ensuring that every new building constructed and every renovation carried out by 2030 meets zero-emission standards.

The New Democratic, Bloc Québécois and Green parties intend to immediately end federal subsidies to the fossil fuel sector.
« Il faut premièrement reconnaître qu’il: “First, we have to recognize that this is an emergency. We have to act quickly and start taking radical steps right now if we want to avoid catastrophe. Right now, as the most recent report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) states, we are heading toward catastrophe,” warns Jean-François Boisvert. “If the trend continues, we’re going to see an increase in the average global temperature of 3 to 4 degrees. That would be downright catastrophic for almost every country.” Asked about the jobs currently in the fossil fuel industries that could be lost during a green transition, a justification the Conservative Party uses to keep supporting these sectors, the president of Coalition Climat Montréal (CCM) is firm. In his view, an energy transition that includes these workers is possible. “What the parties are proposing are peripheral measures that don’t attack the heart of the problem, and in Canada, that’s fossil energy. We have to abandon this form of energy within 20 years. As long as we don’t do that, I don’t believe we can solve the climate issue,” laments Mr. Boisvert. “If we want a just transition that doesn’t penalize workers, there’s a way to get there, but we have to address the problem in its full scope, and that’s not what the main parties are doing.”
Le militant trouve que la cible de 60% d: The activist finds that the Green Party’s target of a 60% emissions reduction by 2030 is a good start, but says there needs to be an action plan for gradually reducing emissions. “The goal is to reach carbon neutrality by 2050. To do that, you have to aim for a gradual reduction. With the Green Party’s target, that would be realistic,” he says, adding that his organization is calling for carbon neutrality as early as possible. “You also need an action plan to get there, otherwise they’re just numbers. It’s also important to have a carbon budget that sets how much Canada can emit by 2050.” To do this, he is asking candidates to carry out annual inventories of the amount of carbon emitted, something that is rarely done at the moment. He believes this measure is essential, since 2050 is just around the corner. Mr. Boisvert also believes in citizen participation in the fight against the climate crisis. “Our organization believes that involving citizens in the process will make it more democratic, because they’ll have a chance to speak up and contribute to a green transition,” he says. He believes citizen participation allows those who are most directly affected to have their concerns taken into account. The CCM president feels that this participation ensures the most marginalized people are not forgotten. “Low-income people have to work long hours and have to take care of their children.
Ces gens-là n’ont pas nécessairement le: These people don’t necessarily have the time to get involved in green transition groups, but it’s still essential to take their demands into account,” explains Mr. Boisvert. “That’s how I see an inclusive climate movement that doesn’t penalize these people.” As an example, he points out that banning gas-powered cars risks penalizing the most marginalized people, because they live in neighbourhoods where public transit networks are often less developed. For the activist, federal public transit strategies must take those neighbourhoods into account. In his view, citizen participation can also provide climate solutions adapted to the distinct local realities of different municipalities across the country. Nicolas Chevalier is an organizer at Leap Montreal, a group that fights for intersectional environmental justice. They believe that of all the main parties, the New Democratic Party has the best environmental platform. “Their platform supports an ecological transition that doesn’t depend on the private sector and market forces. Their suggestions, like increased demand for public transit and plans for active transportation such as cycling, fall under the public sector,” they elaborate.
« D’une façon globale, leur plan est plu: “Overall, their plan is more democratic and inclusive for citizens. I like the Green Party’s platform less because it’s very focused on market solutions that rely on technology and innovation. Economic growth is all over their platform.” The organizer feels it is problematic that none of the five main federal parties question economic growth. According to Chevalier, it is one of the main causes of climate change.
« Les partis conservateurs, libéraux, et: “The Conservative, Liberal and Green parties promote economic growth as a way to save the environment. In my view, that’s not really possible,” they say. Even though the activist believes the New Democrats have the best environmental platform of the main parties, they think all the parties are very far from the demands of environmental and social justice activists. The organizer is firm about the root of environmental problems, which, in their view, lies in the capitalist structure of Canada’s current economy. They call for the federal government to fully divest from fossil fuels and invest in public services. Nicolas Chevalier also views the promises of investment in renewable energy and the jobs created in those sectors with skepticism. “Even the New Democratic Party, which has the least bad platform, doesn’t acknowledge that the causes of climate change are capitalism and colonialism,” they say indignantly. “When we talk about a transition to clean energy, it obscures the continued extraction of minerals, a practice that perpetuates the exploitation of natural resources and the theft of Indigenous land.”
Iel croit plutôt que les emplois verts s: Instead, they believe green jobs are found in low-carbon sectors, such as health care.
Iel est insatisfait du Parti libéral qui: They are dissatisfied with the Liberal Party, which does not grant Indigenous peoples, the guardians of the land, a right to free, prior and informed consent in environmental projects that directly affect their territories. “They swap the word ‘consent’ for the word ‘consultation,’ and they clearly specify that it’s not a right of veto,” they lament.
Plusieurs groupes autochtones abondent d: Several Indigenous groups echo Nicolas Chevalier’s views. In March 2021, Indigenous Climate Action published a report criticizing the fact that Canadian environmental policy systematically excludes Indigenous nations. The report is extremely harsh toward the Pan-Canadian Framework on Clean Growth and Climate Change (PCF), a plan published in 2019, and A Healthy Environment and a Healthy Economy (HEHE), another plan published in 2020. The authors, nêhiyaw-iskwêw researcher Rebecca Sinclair and non-Indigenous researcher Dr. Jen Gobby, decried the fact that Indigenous peoples were denied full membership in the working groups that developed these environmental strategies.
lles ont qualifié ce geste d’acte hypocr: They called this an act of hypocrisy, since the PCF clearly states that Indigenous ecological knowledge is key to solving the climate crisis. When they asked officials why they were refused, the officials confided anonymously that two provinces had blocked full Indigenous participation in these working groups. They would not name the provinces. Ms. Sinclair and Dr. Gobby also found that the process of developing these Canadian environmental plans does not respect the Indigenous right to self-determination and consent upheld by the United Nations, the calls of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, and Justin Trudeau’s promises of 2015. The two researchers found that the inclusion of Indigenous peoples in the PCF is largely superficial. The plan does not give them a say over the carbon pricing process, which goes against the principle of Indigenous sovereignty over their own territories. What’s more, they cannot benefit from carbon tax credits because many do not pay taxes. The researchers also fear that carbon taxes will cause food prices to rise, worsening the food crisis affecting many communities, particularly those in the Far North.
Mme Sinclair et Dr. Gobby ont aussi trou: Ms. Sinclair and Dr. Gobby also found that the PCF’s transportation measures neglect Indigenous communities. According to them, many remote Indigenous communities have no access to a functioning public transit network or to a network of charging stations for electric cars. In addition, many Indigenous people cannot afford to buy an electric car because of their high cost. They are particularly harsh toward the renewable energy plans proposed by the PCF, many of which are similar to those proposed by the main federal parties. The researchers judge that hydroelectric dams, cited as a solution by the Liberal, New Democratic, Bloc Québécois and Green parties, have deeply harmful consequences for many communities. In Manitoba and Quebec, the past construction of hydroelectric dams flooded several Indigenous communities, permanently destroyed ecosystems, and forced many Indigenous people to relocate. Asked about this, Karine Lafontaine, a representative of the Bloc Québécois, told us that the federal government is not responsible for setting up renewable resource development projects. “However, the Bloc Québécois supported Bill C-15, which implements the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, including the notion of free, prior and informed consent, at every stage,” she replied in an email.
« Ce sont aux entreprises qui entament d: “It is up to the companies undertaking hydro resource development projects to seek social acceptability and come to an agreement with the First Nations concerned in order to obtain their free, prior and informed consent by working in partnership with them.” The Liberal, New Democratic and Green parties did not respond to our interview request. Ms. Sinclair and Dr. Gobby believe the political parties’ emphasis on renewable energy is misguided, because these solutions are still focused on the exploitation of natural resources. According to them, the exploitation of natural resources is a fundamental principle of a capitalist and colonialist economy, which they consider to be the true cause of the climate crisis.
Le plus récent rapport du GIEC corrobore: The most recent IPCC report backs up their view, stating that the climate crisis is a problem of values and power imbalances, not a lack of renewable technologies. The two researchers are also skeptical of the effectiveness of the IPCAs, championed by the Conservative, Liberal and Green parties. They believe this solution can work only if the federal government is prepared to provide adequate funding and a position of power to Indigenous peoples to carry out these projects successfully. Given the chronic underfunding of Indigenous initiatives and the forced displacement in the past of many Indigenous communities that could no longer live on a natural territory newly declared protected, the researchers doubt that IPCAs are an adequate solution.
Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami (ITK), un organi: Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami (ITK), a national organization representing the 65,000 Inuit in Canada, has also published a report titled Inuit Priorities for Canada’s Climate Strategy (IPCCS). In this report, ITK highlights the particular needs of communities living in the Canadian Arctic, a region that is warming two to three times faster than the rest of the country. The IPCCS sounds the alarm about the rapid melting of sea ice and permafrost, two natural features that are a source of food, learning, memories and knowledge for the Inuit. According to ITK, the disappearance of these two features would mean the disappearance of the Inuit way of life and culture.
L’ITK revendique des nouveaux protocoles: ITK is calling for new safety protocols for Inuit hunters, on whom most families depend for their food security, because they can no longer rely on traditional routes, which are being altered by climate change. These protocols are all the more urgent since 63% of Inuit families currently experience food insecurity because of the high cost of living in the Far North and the climate disruptions affecting hunters. ITK is also calling for an energy independence plan that takes into account northern realities such as the absence of roads passable year-round, the lack of telecommunications infrastructure and harsh weather conditions. The Inuit community also wants a significant place in international climate negotiations, because it is among those most affected by climate change. Daniel Gladu Kanu, director of the Lake Winnipeg Indigenous Collective (LWIC), has had enough of seeing First Nations excluded from environmental solutions.
« Les partis ne se sont pas assurés que: “The parties haven’t made sure that Indigenous sovereignty is an integral part of the IPCAs. Right now, IPCAs are still under the authority of Parks Canada,” laments Mr. Kanu, an Anishinaabe-Métis from the Animakee Wa Zhing area. “So Parks Canada can form partnerships with us, but the final decision is theirs.” For the LWIC director, this situation is repeated in many environmental initiatives. A project affecting Indigenous territories takes shape in the federal government, and Indigenous people are consulted only once the project is well underway. At that stage, it is very difficult for them to ask for changes. “There was a project in Manitoba meant to counter climate change by diverting the waters of a lake.
Mais ces eaux se sont déversées dans plu: But those waters spilled into several Indigenous communities, a disaster amounting to a billion dollars in damage,” explains Mr. Kanu, as an example of the lack of consultation. “First Nations weren’t consulted about it. Some of us still can’t go back home because of that project.” That is why he is very harsh toward those who consider hydroelectric power a green solution. It reminds him of the big dam projects that were started in the 1970s and flooded several Indigenous communities. “There were people who had less than a week to gather all their belongings and move. And their homes were flooded the following week,” he recalls sadly.
« Plus récemment, il y a eu plus de cons: “More recently, there’s been more consultation with Indigenous peoples on this, but our demands are still mostly ignored. The projects get approved, there have been a few compensation measures, but communities were displaced all the same. Those are the impacts of hydroelectricity, which is often considered a green energy.” Mr. Kanu is calling for First Nations to have a greater say in decisions made as part of project development. For him, since these projects are on the territory where Indigenous people get their food and their health care in the form of medicinal plants, they must be the main decision-makers.
M. Kanu croit aussi que les autochtones: Mr. Kanu also believes that Indigenous people should benefit from the exploitation of natural resources, which takes place mainly on their territories. The director of LWIC sees systemic racism as the source of all these problems. In his view, Indigenous people experience racism when they are consulted on environmental projects, because many public servants are not trained to work with them. It doesn’t help that the few Indigenous staff members in public departments dedicated to environmental issues don’t have enough seniority to make decisions that are crucial for Indigenous people. What’s more, Indigenous ecological knowledge is not given the same weight as science in the courts that rule on environmental decisions.
« Il n’y a pas de solutions environnemen: “There are no environmental solutions that exclude Indigenous peoples. That includes climate change, the protection of waterways and ecosystems,” he concludes. “Indigenous people have lived on this land for a long time and have accumulated knowledge that is essential for the future.”
